To subpoena someone means to officially and legally command them — through a written court order — to either show up and give testimony in a legal proceeding, or to hand over specific documents, records, or other evidence. It is not a request. It is not an invitation. It is a formal legal demand backed by the power of a court.

When someone is subpoenaed, they have no legal right to simply say "no, thanks." Compliance is required by law.

Think of it this way: imagine a court case is happening and a judge or lawyer needs a specific person to come in and speak, or needs a company to hand over its financial records. They cannot just call that person up and hope they agree. Instead, the court issues a formal written document — called a subpoena — that legally forces that person or organization to comply. The act of issuing and serving that document to someone is to subpoena them.

So in a sentence: "The prosecutor subpoenaed the bank for its transaction records." This means the prosecutor obtained a legal court order forcing the bank to produce those records.
The Two Things a Subpoena Can Command

When used as a verb, "to subpoena" almost always falls into one of two situations:

1. Subpoenaing a person to testify. This means legally compelling a person to appear — usually in court, before a grand jury, or in a deposition — and answer questions under oath. For example, if you witnessed a crime, a lawyer can subpoena you to come to court and share what you saw, even if you'd rather stay home. You don't get to opt out.

2. Subpoenaing documents, records, or objects. This means legally compelling a person, a company, or an organization to hand over specific physical or digital materials relevant to a case. For example, a lawyer investigating a fraud case might subpoena a company's internal emails, a hospital's medical records, or a phone company's call logs. The target must locate and produce those materials within a specified deadline.

In both cases, the verb "to subpoena" describes the act of issuing and delivering that legal command.

Not just anyone can subpoena someone. This power belongs to legal authorities — most commonly courts and judges, but also legislative bodies (like a congressional committee investigating something), grand juries, and in many systems, attorneys who are engaged in active litigation. A regular citizen cannot subpoena another person. The authority must come from a recognized legal institution.
What Happens If You Ignore a Subpoena?

This is where the real teeth of the word come in. Because a subpoena is a court order, ignoring it is a serious offense. If you are subpoenaed and you simply don't show up or refuse to comply, you can be held in contempt of court — meaning the court treats your defiance as an act of disrespect toward the legal system itself. The consequences can include fines, or even jail time, until you comply. This is what separates a subpoena from a polite ask — it carries genuine legal force.
A Few Real-World Scenarios to Make It Concrete

• A company executive is subpoenaed to testify before Congress about data privacy violations. She must appear and answer questions, regardless of whether she wants to.
  • During a divorce case, a lawyer subpoenas the other spouse's bank account records to prove hidden income.
  • In a criminal trial, the defense attorney subpoenas a key eyewitness who has been reluctant to cooperate, ensuring that person must appear in court and testify.
  • A journalist is subpoenaed to reveal the identity of a confidential source in a lawsuit. (This is controversial and often legally contested, but it illustrates the reach of a subpoena.)
One Important Nuance: Being Subpoenaed Does NOT Mean You're in Trouble

Many people confuse being subpoenaed with being accused of something. That is a misconception worth clearing up. When you are subpoenaed, it simply means the legal system needs information from you — your testimony or your records. You might be subpoenaed as a neutral witness, as a bystander, or as a record-keeper. Being subpoenaed does not mean you are suspected of wrongdoing. You are not being charged with anything. You are being commanded to contribute information to a legal proceeding.

That said, once you are on the stand (if subpoenaed to testify), you are under oath — meaning you must tell the truth. Lying under oath after being subpoenaed is a separate crime called perjury.

To subpoena is ultimately an exercise of legal power — the court system's ability to reach out and compel participation. It ensures that legal proceedings can access the witnesses and evidence they need, even from unwilling parties. Without this power, people could simply refuse to cooperate with courts, and the justice system would struggle to function. The subpoena is the mechanism that makes legal truth-seeking possible even when cooperation isn't voluntary.
